text:
It was Monsieur Lheureux, the merchant, who had undertaken the commission; this gave him the opportunity to visit Emma frequently. He talked with her about the new arrivals from Paris, about a thousand feminine curiosities, made himself very obliging, and never asked for money. Emma surrendered herself to this ease of satisfying all her whims. Thus, she wanted to have, in order to give it to Rodolphe, a very fine riding crop that was in an umbrella shop in Rouen. The following week, Monsieur Lheureux set it down for her on her table.

But the next day he came to her with a bill for two hundred and seventy francs, not counting the centimes. Emma was very embarrassed: all the drawers of the writing desk were empty; they owed Lestiboudois more than a fortnight’s wages, the servant two quarters’ wages, and a great many other things besides, while Bovary was impatiently awaiting a remittance from Monsieur Derozerays, who was in the habit of paying him every year around Saint Peter’s Day.

At first she managed to send Lheureux away; at last he lost patience; people were pressing him, his capital was tied up, and if some of what was owed him did not come in, he would be forced to take back from her all the merchandise she had bought.

“Ah! Take it back!” said Emma.

“Oh! You are joking!” he replied. “Only, the one thing I regret is the riding crop. Upon my word! I shall ask Monsieur for it back.”

“No! No!” she said.

“Ah! I have you now!” thought Lheureux.

And, certain of his discovery, he went out, repeating under his breath and with his usual little hiss:

“Very well! We shall see! We shall see!”

She was wondering how to get out of the predicament when the cook came in and placed on the mantelpiece a small roll of blue paper from Monsieur Derozerays. Emma pounced on it and opened it. There were fifteen napoleons. It was the payment. She heard Charles on the stairs; she threw the gold into the back of her drawer and took out the key.

Three days later, Lheureux reappeared.

“I have an arrangement to propose to you,” he said. “If, instead of the agreed sum, you would be willing to take...”

“Here it is,” she said, placing fourteen napoleons in his hand.

The merchant was astounded. Then, to conceal his disappointment, he poured forth apologies and offers of service, all of which Emma refused; afterward she stood for several minutes fingering in the pocket of her apron the two five-franc coins he had given her back. She promised herself that she would economize, so as to pay them back later...

“Oh, nonsense!” she thought. “He will not think of it again.”

Besides the riding crop with its silver-gilt knob, Rodolphe had received a seal bearing this motto: _Love in the heart_; in addition, a scarf to use as a muffler, and finally a cigar case exactly like the Viscount’s, which Charles had once picked up on the road and which Emma had kept. Yet these gifts humiliated him. He refused several of them; she insisted, and Rodolphe ended by yielding, finding her tyrannical and too intrusive.

Then she had strange notions:

“When midnight strikes,” she would say, “you will think of me!”

And if he admitted that he had not thought of it, there would be reproaches in abundance, always ending with the eternal words:

“Do you love me?”

“Why, yes, I love you!” he would answer.

“A great deal?”

“Certainly!”

“You have not loved others, have you?”

“Do you think you took me as a virgin?” he would exclaim, laughing.

Emma would weep, and he would try to console her, embellishing his protestations with puns.

“Oh! It is because I love you!” she would resume. “I love you so much that I cannot do without you, you know? Sometimes I long to see you again so fiercely that all love’s furies tear me apart. I ask myself: ‘Where is he? Perhaps he is talking to other women? They smile at him, he draws nearer...’ Oh! No, is that not so, none of them pleases you? There are women more beautiful; but I know how to love better! I am your servant and your concubine! You are my king, my idol! You are good! You are handsome! You are intelligent! You are strong!”

He had heard these things said to him so many times that they held nothing original for him. Emma was like all mistresses; and the charm of novelty, gradually falling away like a garment, laid bare the eternal monotony of passion, which always has the same forms and the same language. This man, so full of experience, did not distinguish the dissimilarity of feelings beneath the similarity of expressions. Because wanton or venal lips had murmured similar phrases to him, he had little faith in the candor of these; one had to discount them, he thought, exaggerated speeches concealing mediocre affections; as though the fullness of the soul did not sometimes overflow through the emptiest metaphors, since no one can ever give the exact measure of his needs, his conceptions, or his sufferings, and human speech is like a cracked cauldron on which we beat out tunes to make bears dance when we would like to move the stars to pity.

But with that critical superiority belonging to one who, in any involvement whatsoever, holds himself back, Rodolphe perceived in this love other pleasures to exploit. He considered all modesty inconvenient. He treated her without ceremony. He made of her something pliant and corrupt. It was a kind of mindless attachment, full of admiration for him, of sensual pleasures for her, a bliss that numbed her; and her soul sank into that intoxication and drowned there, shriveled like the Duke of Clarence in his butt of malmsey.

Through the effect of her amorous habits alone, Madame Bovary’s manner changed. Her glances became bolder, her speech freer; she even had the impropriety to walk about with Monsieur Rodolphe, a cigarette in her mouth, as though to flout the world; finally, those who still had doubts doubted no longer when, one day, she was seen getting down from the Hirondelle, her waist confined in a waistcoat like a man’s; and Madame Bovary senior, who, after a dreadful scene with her husband, had come to seek refuge at her son’s house, was not the least scandalized of the respectable women. Many other things displeased her: first, Charles had not heeded her advice about forbidding novels; then, the way the household was run displeased her; she ventured to make comments, and tempers flared, particularly on one occasion concerning Félicité.

The previous evening, as Madame Bovary senior was crossing the corridor, she had caught her in the company of a man, a man with a brown collar, about forty years old, who, at the sound of her footsteps, had quickly slipped out of the kitchen. Emma then began to laugh; but the good lady flew into a rage, declaring that unless one meant to make a mockery of morality, one ought to keep watch over the morals of one’s servants.
